units.text: At Umm Mabad's Two Tents
What happened at Umm Mabad's, and how did she describe to her husband the visitor who had left?

We follow the party's stop at Umm Mabad's as told in the report of Hubaysh ibn Khalid: their request for food, the sheep that remained in the tent, and the conversation between husband and wife after the guests left. The accompanying readings help explain the words of the description and present Ibn Kathir's and al-Albani's comments on the report's transmission routes, without treating all its chains and wordings as agreed upon.
The sheep left in the tent

In Hubaysh ibn Khalid's report, the Prophet ﷺ passed by the two tents of Umm Mabad of Khuzaa on the Hijrah route, accompanied by Abu Bakr, Amir ibn Fuhayrah, and their guide Abd Allah ibn Urayqit (أريقط). Umm Mabad sat in the forecourt of her tent, giving people drink and food; but they found none of the meat and dates they asked to buy from her.

The Prophet ﷺ saw a sheep in the tent and asked Umm Mabad about it. Exhaustion had kept it from following the flock, so it remained there. He asked whether it had any milk, and she replied, “It is too exhausted for that.” Then he asked her permission: “Will you allow me to milk it?” She permitted him to do so if he saw that it could be milked.
Milking and sharing the drink

The Prophet ﷺ had the sheep brought, stroked its udder with his hand, invoked Allah's name, and prayed. The sheep, from which Umm Mabad had expected no milk, began to give milk; he called for a vessel and milked a plentiful amount into it. He gave Umm Mabad drink until she was satisfied, then his companions until they were satisfied, and drank last himself.

The milking did not end with their drinking: he milked it a second time until he filled the vessel. This time he left it with Umm Mabad. The party then departed, leaving her the milk her husband would find on his return.
Abu Mabad's question
After they left, her husband Abu Mabad arrived driving lean goats. He was astonished to see the milk and asked her where it had come from, saying there was no milk-giving sheep in the household.
Umm Mabad told him of a man who had passed by them and called him “a blessed man.” He asked her to describe him, and she began relating what she had seen of his appearance and heard of his speech.
The visitor as she described him

She described to him a man with a handsome face, a thick beard, and a stature between tall and short; handsome from afar and pleasing close up. When silent he had dignity, and when he spoke, splendor. She then described the sweetness of his speech, likening his words to an ordered string of beads descending one after another.
She did not describe him alone: she also described his companions around him. When he spoke they listened to his words, and when he gave an order they hastened to carry it out.

When Abu Mabad heard her description, he connected the visitor with what they had heard in Makkah about the man of Quraysh. He said he had considered accompanying him and would do so if he found a way. He had not witnessed the visit, but heard his wife's description of the man who had come to her.
Hospitality amid scarcity

The report says both that Umm Mabad gave people food and drink and that she had none of the requested meat and dates. This was not a refusal to feed guests; the party was short of provisions and in hardship. Abu Ubayd, as quoted by Abu Nuaym, explains murmil as someone whose provisions have run out, and musnitin as people struck by a hard year—that is, crisis and famine.
What does “sweetness of speech” describe?

The image of beads on a string descending conveys the order and succession of his words, not just a beautiful voice. In Abu Ubayd's explanation, nazr means little and hadhr means much; the description is a middle course between them. It then turns to the effect of his speech on his companions: they listen to him and hasten to do what he commands. The portrait thus expands from the visitor's appearance to his speech and his relationship with those around him.
One chain and the combined routes

Ibn Kathir says that the story is well known and transmitted through routes that reinforce one another. Al-Albani, however, in the selected footnote to Hidayat al-Ruwat, objects to the soundness of this chain because of Hisham ibn Hubaysh: he was listed in al-Jarh wa-l-Tadil without any criticism or endorsement, and no transmitter from him besides his son was mentioned. Al-Albani does not rule out corroboration: he says the report may rise to hasan (good) or sahih (sound) by routes cited by al-Hakim.

The distinction is between assessing a particular chain and strengthening a report through multiple routes. We therefore do not turn al-Albani's objection into a categorical denial of the story, or Ibn Kathir's remark into a detailed authentication of every wording. The account follows Hubaysh's report in Abu Nuaym; this chapter is neither a comprehensive study of all routes nor a new judgment on its chain.
Who is speaking on the source page?

In the selected pages of Hidayat al-Ruwat, the editor first reproduces the report's text from al-Mishkat, then comes Ibn Hajar's attribution to al-Bayhaqi, followed by al-Albani's footnote. Ali al-Halabi explains in his editorial introduction that he took al-Albani's source references and comments to append to the book. The objection to the chain should therefore not be attributed to Ibn Hajar simply because his name appears on the book.

Why did the party not buy meat and dates from Umm Mabad?
The report says that what they requested was unavailable, although it also describes Umm Mabad as giving people food and drink.
This question is limited to Hubaysh's report in Abu Nuaym, as followed in this chapter's account.
Because they disagreed with her over the price.
The report mentions no disagreement about the price; it says she did not have what they requested.
Because she did not have what they requested.
Yes. They asked to buy food but found no meat or dates with her.
Because they waited for her husband to return and sell it to them.
Abu Mabad returned after they left; the report does not say they delayed their purchase for him.
What kept the sheep in the tent instead of going out with the flock?
Exhaustion kept it there; this also explains Umm Mabad's response when asked about its milk.
This question is limited to Hubaysh's report in Abu Nuaym, as followed in this chapter's account.
Exhaustion that prevented it from keeping up with the flock.
Yes. Umm Mabad says exhaustion left it behind the flock.
It had been kept ready to milk when guests arrived.
Umm Mabad did not expect milk from it; she said it was too exhausted for that.
It had been put up for sale to passersby.
The party asked for meat and dates, but the report attributes this sheep's remaining behind to exhaustion, not to its being offered for sale.
After asking about the sheep's milk, what did the Prophet ﷺ ask Umm Mabad for?
He first asked about the sheep's condition, then requested permission to milk it; she permitted him if he found milk in it.
This question is limited to Hubaysh's report in Abu Nuaym, as followed in this chapter's account.
That she bring the flock that was away from the tent.
The exchange concerned milking the sheep already there, not fetching the flock.
That she sell him the sheep in the tent.
The request reported here was for permission to milk it, not to buy it.
That she allow him to milk the sheep.
Yes. He milked it after asking and receiving her permission.
In what order does the report say they drank the milk?
The Prophet ﷺ served Umm Mabad first, then his companions, and drank last.
This question is limited to Hubaysh's report in Abu Nuaym, as followed in this chapter's account.
His companions, then Umm Mabad, then he himself.
He gave Umm Mabad milk before serving his companions.
Umm Mabad, then his companions, then he himself.
Yes. He gave her drink until she was satisfied, then his companions until they were satisfied, and drank last.
He himself, then Umm Mabad, then his companions.
The report explicitly says he drank last, not first.
Where did the milk Abu Mabad found after the party left come from?
After they drank, the Prophet ﷺ milked the sheep again until he filled the vessel and left it with Umm Mabad.
This question is limited to Hubaysh's report in Abu Nuaym, as followed in this chapter's account.
Abu Mabad brought it back with the flock.
Abu Mabad found the milk already there and was surprised; the report does not say he brought it.
Umm Mabad had stored it before their arrival.
The report links the vessel left behind to the second milking, not to milk stored before the visit.
The Prophet ﷺ filled the vessel in a second milking and left it with her.
Yes. The report mentions more than just the milk they drank.
What did Umm Mabad include in her description of the visitor?
Her description moves from his face and stature to his speech and dignity, and then to his companions' attentiveness and quick response.
This question is limited to Hubaysh's report in Abu Nuaym, as followed in this chapter's account.
His appearance alone, without his speech or companions.
The report describes his speech, dignity, and companions' attention, not just his appearance.
His speech alone, without his appearance or companions.
The sweetness of his speech is part of a portrait that also includes his appearance and companions.
His appearance, speech, and relationship with his companions.
Yes. She spoke of his beauty, dignity, sweet speech, and what she observed of his companions.
How did Abu Mabad connect the visitor to the man of Quraysh?
Umm Mabad described the visit, and Abu Mabad heard her account before saying the visitor was the man of Quraysh whose story had reached them.
This question is limited to Hubaysh's report in Abu Nuaym, as followed in this chapter's account.
By meeting him in person before the party left.
Abu Mabad returned after their departure and then asked his wife about the visitor.
From his wife's description after he asked her.
Yes. His identification of the man of Quraysh follows Umm Mabad's description.
From a letter the party left with Umm Mabad.
What they left here was a vessel of milk; this report mentions no letter identifying the visitor.
How does Abu Ubayd explain the description of speech as neither nazr (نزر) nor hadhr (هذر)?
Abu Ubayd explains nazr (نزر) as little and hadhr (هذر) as much, and says that the intended meaning is a middle course between the two.
Optional study of Abu Ubayd's explanation as quoted by Abu Nuaym; these explanatory words are not Umm Mabad's own.
Abundant speech that only improves the longer it goes on.
He explains hadhr as much and describes a middle course between little and much.
Speech that follows a middle course between little and much.
Yes. This is the meaning given by the selected explanation.
A low voice that the companions cannot hear.
The explanation concerns the amount of speech, not its volume or whether it can be heard.
What is the difference between Ibn Kathir's statement and al-Albani's comment in the two selected readings?
Strengthening the story by several routes does not mean that each chain is sound on its own. Al-Albani's comment does not stop at an objection: he then allows for possible corroboration.
This comparison concerns only these two passages, not an exhaustive account of critics' judgments or an independent ruling on the chain.
Ibn Kathir authenticates every wording, while al-Albani rejects the entire story.
The first speaks of routes reinforcing the story; the second allows for possible corroboration after objecting to the chain.
Both unreservedly authenticate this particular chain.
Al-Albani expressly objects to the soundness of this chain because of Hisham ibn Hubaysh's status.
Ibn Kathir regards the story as reinforced by its routes; al-Albani objects to the chain but mentions possible corroboration.
Yes. The scope and degree of certainty of each statement remain distinct.
To whom is the objection to the soundness of the chain of Umm Mabad's report attributed in the selected footnote to Hidayat al-Ruwat?
Al-Albani's comment was appended to the book; the introduction identifies its author, so not everything on the page should be attributed to the author of the main text.
Optional study of the authors' and editor's distinct voices in this edition, not new historical evidence about the encounter.
Ibn Hajar, author of Hidayat al-Ruwat.
The selected statement by Ibn Hajar attributes the report to al-Bayhaqi; the objection appears in the appended footnote.
Ali al-Halabi, editor of this edition.
Al-Halabi explains in the introduction that he took his teacher's source references and comments to append to the book.
Al-Albani, author of the appended comment.
Yes. The edition's details and introduction distinguish the source of the footnote from the book's main text.
This wording and comparison are limited internal work, not independent linguistic or historical approval or permission to publish.

This batch did not cover every route of the Umm Mabad report or all critics’ judgments on them; the rest of the road-encounter family remains for expansion. Placing this chapter after Suraqa is a reading order, not a determination of the sequence of those two events.

The digital spellings have been preserved, including نَذْز in Abu Nuaym’s text versus نَزْر in Abu Ubayd’s explanation and the disturbed wording at the end of al-Albani’s footnote; they have not been checked against a print copy or silently corrected in the quotation. Explaining the meaning does not replace the original.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had it brought, stroked its udder with his hand, named Allah ﷿ and prayed for her regarding her sheep. It spread its legs for him, gave milk, and chewed the cud. He called for a vessel that would suffice the group and milked copiously into it until foam rose over it. Then he gave her drink until she had enough, and his companions until they had enough; then he ﷺ drank last. Then they drank to their fill, and he milked it a second time after the first until he filled the vessel, left it with her, entered into a pledge with her, and they departed.

a long neck and thick beard, with arched eyebrows that met. When silent, he bore dignity; when he spoke, he rose in stature and splendor covered him. From afar he was the most beautiful and splendid of people, and from near the most pleasing and handsome. His speech was sweet and distinct, neither نَذْز nor excessive; it was as though his words were beads in a string descending.
